transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Let's get started. As you know, we have a preliminary-injunction hearing in three weeks, and I need to approve our response strategy before the motion papers are finalized. Before I sign off on anything, I need each of you to put your cards on the table — any material evidence you've uncovered, any business constraints I should be aware of, and any proposed filing commitments you think we need to make. I don't want surprises after we've already committed to a strategy. Who wants to go first?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: Marisol, I need to disclose something important before we finalize the strategy. After the strategy-memo cutoff, I was reviewing a forensic image that was delivered late, and I found two critical things: first, the former employee's signed confidentiality agreement, and second, logs showing that 4,800 files — including source code and deployment scripts — were copied to an external drive. These supplemental findings have not yet been added to the motion outline. In my view, the signed agreement and the scale of the 4,800-file evidence strengthen our case significantly and make an expedited forensic inspection of the competitor's systems necessary. I recommend we request that inspection in the motion and file a supplemental-evidence filing to incorporate these findings.

Thank you both. Ethan, the signed confidentiality agreement and the 4,800-file copy logs are significant — that's exactly the kind of evidence that strengthens our likelihood-of-success argument. I agree we need to incorporate those findings, but I want to think carefully about the timing and mechanics of a supplemental filing. We need to make sure the court has these materials before the hearing without creating procedural vulnerability.

Nadia, the 30-day customer-transition carve-out is noted as a hard condition. That actually complicates things — we need to frame the injunction in a way that stops the competitor's ongoing use of our client's confidential software while giving existing customers a runway to transition. That's a narrower injunction than a straight shutdown, and it affects how we draft the proposed order.

Before I approve the strategy, I need to reconcile these two pieces: Ethan is pushing for an expedited forensic inspection of the competitor's systems, and Nadia's client constraint means we can't simply seek to shut everything down. I also need to know — does anyone else have evidence or constraints I haven't heard yet? I want the full picture before I commit us to a filing strategy.
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: Marisol, to address your concern about reconciling the forensic inspection with Nadia's 30-day transition carve-out — I think these two pieces are actually compatible. The expedited forensic inspection would help us prove that the competitor's systems contain our client's confidential software, which strengthens the likelihood-of-success showing the court needs for a preliminary injunction. The 30-day transition window, on the other hand, shapes the scope of the remedy we're requesting — it's about what the proposed order looks like, not about whether we can demonstrate the underlying infringement. So we can pursue the forensic inspection to build our evidentiary record while simultaneously drafting the proposed order with the customer-transition carve-out Nadia described. On the procedural timing question you raised — I'd recommend we file the supplemental-evidence filing as soon as possible, ideally within the next week, so the court has the signed confidentiality agreement and the 4,800-file copy logs well before the hearing. That gives us adequate lead time and minimizes any argument from opposing counsel that we're springing new evidence at the eleventh hour. I'm happy to start drafting the supplemental filing and the forensic-inspection request language this week if you're inclined to approve that approach.

transcript.text: Ethan, I agree the forensic inspection and the transition carve-out are compatible — one goes to likelihood of success, the other to the scope of the remedy. I'm inclined to approve the approach with two conditions. First, the supplemental-evidence filing needs to go in within the next week, as you suggested, and it should include both the signed confidentiality agreement and the 4,800-file copy logs with a clear chain-of-custody declaration. Second, the forensic-inspection request needs to be narrowly tailored — we're asking the court for access to the competitor's systems to identify our client's confidential software, not a fishing expedition. Opposing counsel will fight this, so the proposed order for the inspection needs to be specific about scope, timing, and a neutral third-party vendor if possible. On the injunction itself, the proposed order will include the 30-day customer-transition window for existing hosted customers and will not require a shutdown of the customer-facing service during that period. After 30 days, the competitor must cease all use of the confidential software. If there are no other disclosures — evidence, constraints, or filing commitments — I'm prepared to approve this strategy and move to finalizing the motion papers.

transcript.text: Marisol, I agree to both conditions. I'll also coordinate with Nadia to make sure the injunction language in the proposed order reflects the 30-day customer-transition window and the no-shutdown-during-transition provision. If I can have your sign-off, I'll start drafting the supplemental filing and the forensic-inspection request today and circulate drafts to the team by end of week.
